module_title: Traditional African Cured Meats: Biltong and DroÃ«wors

lessons.title: Biltong Basics: Spices, Vinegar, and Air-Drying
lessons.body:
Biltong is a traditional African cured meat made from beef, game, or ostrich. The key ingredients are coarse salt, brown sugar, coriander seeds, black pepper, and vinegar. For 1 kg of meat, use 20 g coarse salt, 10 g brown sugar, 10 g toasted coriander seeds (crushed), 5 g black pepper, and 100 ml brown vinegar (or apple cider vinegar). The vinegar creates an acidic environment that inhibits harmful bacteria while allowing beneficial enzymes to tenderise the meat. Salt draws out moisture and further protects against spoilage.

You will need a sharp knife, a mixing bowl, a drying rack (or hooks), and a well-ventilated space. Cut the meat into strips about 2 cm thick, 5 cm wide, and as long as you like. Trim off excess fat and sinew. Mix the dry spices together. Dip each strip into vinegar, then rub generously with the spice mix. Layer the spiced strips in a bowl, cover, and refrigerate for 12 to 24 hours. This curing step flavours the meat and starts the preservation process.

After curing, hang the strips to dry. In a dry, breezy climate, you can hang them outdoors under shade cloth or in a dedicated drying box. Air must circulate around each piece. Depending on thickness and humidity, drying takes 3 to 5 days. The biltong is ready when it is firm and dry on the outside but still slightly moist inside. If you prefer it drier, leave it another day. In humid climates, use a fan or a light bulb in a drying box to keep the air moving and prevent mould.

Store finished biltong in a paper bag or breathable container in a cool, dry place. It keeps for weeks. Never store in plastic, as trapped moisture causes mould. With practice, you can adjust spices to your tasteâsome add chilli flakes, garlic powder, or a pinch of bicarbonate of soda to soften the meat. Biltong is high in protein and perfect for snacks, hiking, or selling at local markets.

lessons.title: Making Beef Biltong: Step-by-Step from Raw to Dry
lessons.body:
Start with the right cut. Beef silverside, topside, or rump works best. Choose meat that is fresh, lean, and at least 2 kg. Ask your butcher to cut it into long strips with the grain, about 2 cm thick. Fat should be trimmed but not entirely removedâa little fat adds flavour. You will also need coarse salt, brown sugar, coriander seeds, black pepper, vinegar, and optional Worcestershire sauce. For 2 kg beef: 40 g salt, 20 g sugar, 20 g coriander, 10 g pepper, 200 ml vinegar.

Step 1: Toast coriander seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, then crush coarsely. Mix with salt, sugar, and pepper. Step 2: Pour vinegar into a shallow dish. Dip each meat strip into vinegar, ensuring full coverage. Step 3: Rub the spice mix into the meat on all sides. Place strips in a glass or plastic container, cover, and refrigerate for 24 hours. Turn the meat once after 12 hours. Step 4: Remove from fridge and pat off excess liquid with paper towel. Do not rinse.

Step 5: Hang the strips. Use stainless steel hooks or paper clips (sanitised) to hang meat in a drying box or a cool, dry room with a fan. Space them at least 5 cm apart. Ideal temperature is 15â20Â°C with 50â60% humidity. If humidity is higher, use a fan or dehumidifier. Step 6: Dry for 3 to 5 days. Check daily. The biltong is done when the outside is hard and dark, but the inside is still slightly pink and moist. For wet biltong (more moist), dry 3 days; for dry, 5 days. Step 7: Cut a piece to test. It should be firm but not rock-hard. If mould appears (green or black spots), discard affected pieces and increase airflow.

Once dry, slice thinly against the grain. Store in paper bags or cotton sacks in a cool, dark place. It keeps for 2â4 weeks. For longer storage, vacuum-seal and freeze. This method works for beef, game, or ostrich. With practice, you can scale up for a small business selling biltong at markets or to local shops.

lessons.title: DroÃ«wors: Spiced Dry Sausage from South Africa
lessons.body:
DroÃ«wors is a traditional South African dry sausage, similar to biltong but made with minced meat and spices stuffed into casings. It is a favourite snack and keeps well without refrigeration. The basic recipe for 2 kg of beef (or game) mince: 40 g coarse salt, 20 g brown sugar, 20 g toasted coriander seeds (crushed), 10 g black pepper, 5 g ground cloves, 5 g ground nutmeg, 100 ml brown vinegar, and 10 g baking soda (optional, for tenderness). You will also need natural sheep or hog casings, a sausage stuffer (or a funnel), and a drying rack.

Start by mixing the mince with all dry spices and vinegar. Knead well for 5 minutes until the mixture is sticky. Cover and refrigerate for 2 hours to let flavours blend. Soak casings in warm water for 30 minutes to soften. Rinse inside and out. Stuff the meat mixture into casings, making links about 30 cm long. Do not overstuff, or casings will burst. Tie ends with string. Prick small holes along the sausage with a sterilised needle to release air.

Hang the sausages in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. Ideal conditions: 15â20Â°C, 50â60% humidity, with a gentle breeze. If humid, use a fan or a drying box. Dry for 4 to 7 days. The droÃ«wors is ready when it is firm and dry but still slightly pliable. It should not be brittle. Cut a link to testâinside should be dark red and dry. If mould appears, wipe with vinegar and increase airflow. In very dry climates, 4 days may be enough; in humid areas, up to 10 days.

Once dry, store in paper bags or hang in a cool pantry. It keeps for 3â4 weeks. For longer shelf life, vacuum-seal and freeze. DroÃ«wors can be made from beef, kudu, springbok, or ostrich. Adjust spices to tasteâsome add chilli or garlic. This is a popular product for informal traders because it is lightweight, nutritious, and has a long shelf life. Always maintain hygiene: clean hands, tools, and surfaces to prevent contamination.

lessons.title: Using Game Meats: Kudu, Springbok, and Impala
lessons.body:
Game meats like kudu, springbok, and impala make excellent biltong and droÃ«wors. They are leaner than beef, with a distinct flavour. However, they require careful handling because game animals may carry bacteria. Only use meat from healthy animals, and process it quickly after hunting. If you buy game meat, ensure it comes from a licensed butcher. For 1 kg of game meat, use the same spice mix as beef: 20 g salt, 10 g sugar, 10 g coriander, 5 g pepper, 100 ml vinegar. Game meat benefits from a slightly longer curing timeâup to 36 hoursâto tenderise.

Kudu is a large antelope with dense, dark meat. It is best for biltong because its low fat content dries well. Cut strips 2 cm thick. Springbok is smaller and more tender; its meat is mild and slightly sweet. It makes excellent droÃ«wors. Impala is similar to springbok but slightly larger. For all game, trim off all fat and sinewâgame fat turns rancid quickly. Use vinegar generously to kill surface bacteria. Some hunters add a tablespoon of lemon juice per kg for extra acidity.

Drying game meat takes 3 to 5 days, similar to beef. Because game is lean, it dries faster and can become too hard. Check daily. If the outside is hard but inside still moist, it is perfect. If it becomes brittle, reduce drying time next batch. In humid climates, use a drying box with a fan. Game biltong has a stronger, earthier flavour than beef. It is prized in South Africa and Namibia. You can sell it at a premium price.

For droÃ«wors, mix game mince with beef fat (about 20% fat) to prevent dryness. Otherwise, the sausage will be crumbly. Use the same spices as beef droÃ«wors. Stuff into casings and dry for 4 to 7 days. Game droÃ«wors is a delicacy. Always label your product clearly if selling, and follow local food safety regulations. With practice, you can create a niche market for game biltong and droÃ«wors, especially among tourists and health-conscious customers.

lessons.title: Building a Drying Box for Humid Climates
lessons.body:
In humid climates, air-drying biltong and droÃ«wors is risky because mould grows quickly. A drying box solves this by controlling airflow, temperature, and humidity. You can build a simple box using plywood, plastic sheeting, or a large cardboard box. The box should be at least 60 cm wide, 60 cm deep, and 90 cm tall. You will need a small fan (computer fan or 12V fan), a light bulb (40W) for heat, a hygrometer (to measure humidity), and a thermostat (optional). Total cost: about R500âR800 ($30â$50).

Cut a hole at the bottom for the fan to blow air in, and another hole at the top for air to escape. Cover holes with mesh to keep insects out. Install the fan to circulate air upward. Place the light bulb near the bottom to provide gentle warmthâaim for 25â30Â°C. Too much heat cooks the meat; too little slows drying. Use a hygrometer to monitor humidity. Ideal humidity is 50â60%. If higher, add a small dehumidifier or increase airflow. If lower, place a bowl of water inside. Hang meat from a wooden dowel or stainless steel rod using hooks. Space pieces 5 cm apart.

Run the box in a dry, shaded area. Plug in the fan and light. Check temperature and humidity twice daily. Turn meat occasionally. Drying time in a box is 2 to 4 days, faster than outdoor drying. The box protects against rain, insects, and dust. It also allows you to dry year-round, even in rainy seasons. Clean the box after each batch with vinegar and water to prevent mould spores. Replace the light bulb if it burns out.

For a larger operation, you can build a walk-in drying room with a dehumidifier and exhaust fan. But for home or small business, a box is enough. Always test your first batch: if meat dries unevenly, adjust airflow. If mould appears, increase fan speed and reduce humidity. With a drying box, you can produce consistent biltong and droÃ«wors regardless of weather. This is essential for selling to customers who expect quality.

lessons.title: Packaging and Storing Biltong for Long Shelf Life
lessons.body:
Proper packaging and storage are critical for biltong and droÃ«wors. Even fully dried meat can spoil if exposed to moisture, air, or pests. The goal is to keep it dry, cool, and dark. For short-term storage (up to 4 weeks), use paper bags, cotton sacks, or breathable containers. Never use plastic bags for storageâtrapped moisture causes mould. If you must use plastic, ensure the biltong is bone-dry and add a desiccant packet. For longer storage (3â6 months), vacuum-seal portions and keep them in a cool, dark place or freezer. Vacuum sealing removes air and prevents mould.

For selling, packaging must be attractive and legal. Use food-grade paper bags with a clear window, or vacuum-sealed pouches. Label with product name, ingredients, weight, production date, and expiry date. In South Africa, you need a certificate of acceptability (COA) from your local municipality to sell processed meat. Check your country's regulations. For informal markets, simple paper bags with a sticker are often acceptable. Always wear gloves when handling finished biltong to avoid contamination.

Store biltong in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. Ideal temperature is below 20Â°C. If you live in a hot, humid area, keep it in the fridge or freezer. Biltong can be frozen for up to 6 months without losing quality. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature. DroÃ«wors can be hung in a cool pantry if humidity is low. If it becomes too dry, it will harden; if too moist, it will mould. Check stored products weekly for signs of mould (green, black, or white fuzzy spots). If mould appears, discard the affected piece. Do not just cut it offâmould can spread invisible spores.

For a small business, invest in a vacuum sealer (about R1000âR2000) and a digital scale. Package in 50g, 100g, and 200g portions. Offer different flavours (original, chilli, garlic). Store in a cool room with a dehumidifier if possible. Keep records of production dates and batch numbers. This ensures you can trace any issues. With proper packaging, your biltong can reach customers far from your location, increasing sales and reducing waste.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Biltong & Drowors Production, Safety, and Shelf Life

This practical reference distils the technical essentials of producing biltong and drowors at a semi-commercial scale. It is written for agribusiness operators, small meat processors, and farmer-entrepreneurs who need repeatable results, compliant processes, and a clear view of the cost and quality drivers that determine margin. Whether you are curing beef, game, or a blend, the same physics and microbiology govern the outcome: control water activity (aw), control temperature, control airflow, and control hygiene. Get these four right and you get consistent product, longer shelf life, and fewer losses.

1. The Core Science in One Page

Biltong and drowors are both preserved by a combination of salt, acid (vinegar), drying, andâin the case of droworsâfermentation. The target is to reduce water activity below the level at which spoilage and pathogenic bacteria can grow. For dried meat products, aw below 0.85 is generally regarded as shelf-stable at ambient temperature, while aw below 0.91 inhibits most pathogenic bacteria including Staphylococcus aureus. Salt, sugar, and drying all lower aw; vinegar lowers pH, which adds a second hurdle.

2. Process Parameters That Matter

The single biggest cause of failed batches in humid African climates is insufficient airflow. Drying is a mass-transfer problem: water must move from the interior of the meat to the surface and then be carried away by air. If relative humidity is high and air speed is low, the surface stays wet, mould grows, and case-hardening traps moisture inside. Aim for air speed of 1â2 m/s across the meat surface, relative humidity below 65% where possible, and a temperature of 20â27Â°C. Higher temperatures speed drying but risk fat rancidity and surface hardening.

For drowors, the fermentation step adds complexity. Historically, drowors were made from spiced, salted beef or game offcuts stuffed into natural casings and dried. Modern food safety guidance treats them as a fermented dry sausage, which means you need a controlled fermentation to drop pH below 5.3 within 48 hours, followed by drying to aw below 0.85. Without a starter culture, you rely on the natural flora, which is unpredictable. For commercial production, a Pediococcus pentosaceus or Lactobacillus sakei starter is strongly recommended.

Table 1: Target process parameters for biltong and drowors
Parameter Biltong Drowors Why it matters
Salt concentration (brine %)2.5â3.5% of meat weight2.8â3.2%Water activity reduction, pathogen inhibition
Vinegar (acetic acid)Brown spirit vinegar, 5% acidOften omitted or reducedpH hurdle, surface sanitation
Fermentation pHNot applicable< 5.3 within 48 hInhibits pathogens, enables drying
Drying temperature20â27Â°C18â24Â°CBalance drying speed vs. rancidity
Relative humidity< 65%75â85% (ferment), then < 75% (dry)Controls drying rate and case-hardening
Air speed1â2 m/s0.5â1.5 m/sRemoves boundary layer moisture
Final water activity (aw)< 0.85< 0.85Shelf stability at ambient temperature
Final moisture loss50â60% of raw weight35â45%Yield and texture

Sources: FAO/WHO (2007) Guidelines on the Application of General Principles of Food Hygiene to the Control of Listeria monocytogenes in Ready-to-Eat Foods; Leistner (2000) hurdle technology; South African National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications (NRCS) meat processing guidelines.

3. Spice Blends and Regional Variation

Biltong spice is not a single recipe. Across Southern Africa, the blend shifts with local availability and family tradition. The constant is a balance of salt, acid, and aromatics. A workable commercial baseline for 10 kg of raw beef strips is: 250 g coarse salt, 100 g brown sugar, 40 g cracked black pepper, 30 g toasted coriander seed (crushed), 15 g bicarbonate of soda (optional, for texture), and 250 ml brown spirit vinegar. For drowors, add 5 g ground cloves, 5 g ground nutmeg, and 10 g ground allspice, and reduce the vinegar.

Game meats change the equation. Kudu, springbok, and impala are leaner than beef, with less intramuscular fat. Leaner meat dries faster but can become brittle. Many producers add 5â10% beef fat or a small amount of pork fat to game biltong to improve mouthfeel and reduce breakage. Game also has a stronger, sometimes gamier flavour, so spice blends are often heavier on coriander and pepper to balance it.

Table 2: Comparative composition and drying behaviour of common biltong meats (per 100 g raw, approximate)
Meat Protein (g) Fat (g) Moisture (g) Typical drying time (h) Notes
Beef (silverside)2157348â72Baseline; forgiving
Kudu2327436â60Very lean; add fat
Springbok2237436â60Fine grain; premium
Impala2237436â60Similar to springbok
Ostrich2227530â48Dries fast; watch case-hardening

Sources: FAO (2010) Game meat: a review of the industry and its potential; South African Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD) game meat handling guidelines; USDA FoodData Central (2023). Values are approximate and vary with animal age, diet, and cut.

4. Building a Drying Box for Humid Climates

In coastal or high-rainfall regionsâLagos, Durban, Mombasa, Accraâambient humidity can sit above 80% for weeks. A simple box with a fan is not enough. You need active dehumidification or a heat source that raises the air's moisture-holding capacity. A practical design for 20â30 kg batches uses:

  • An insulated cabinet (50 mm polystyrene or polyurethane panels) with a volume of 1.5â2 mÂ³.
  • A 100â200 W axial fan moving air across the hanging meat at 1â2 m/s.
  • A 300â500 W PTC heater with a thermostat set to 25â28Â°C.
  • A desiccant or compressor dehumidifier rated for at least 10 L/day.
  • An exhaust vent with a adjustable louvre to bleed moisture-laden air.
  • A digital hygrometer/thermometer and, ideally, a data logger.

Run the box at 25Â°C and 55â60% RH for beef biltong. For drowors, start at 22Â°C and 80â85% RH for 48 hours to allow fermentation, then drop to 18Â°C and 70% RH for drying. Never let the surface dry faster than the interiorâif you see a hard shell forming, lower the temperature and raise the humidity slightly.

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE PRODUCING FOR SALE

Biltong and drowors are ready-to-eat (RTE) products. They are not cooked. Any pathogen present on the raw meatâSalmonella, E. coli O157:H7, Listeria monocytogenesâcan survive if the salt, acid, and drying hurdles are insufficient. In South Africa, RTE meat products must comply with SANS 885 and be produced in facilities registered with the NRCS. In the EU and UK, biltong imports must meet EU Regulation 852/2004 and 2073/2005 microbiological criteria. Do not sell product made in a home kitchen without a food safety management system based on HACCP. If you are producing for export, verify the destination country's requirements for RTE dried meat before investing in equipment. When in doubt, test every batch for aw, pH, and Listeria.

5. Packaging and Shelf Life

Properly dried biltong with aw below 0.85 and a pH below 5.5 can achieve 6â12 months shelf life at ambient temperature if packaged correctly. The main enemies after drying are moisture migration, oxygen (rancidity), and light. Use vacuum packaging or high-barrier pouches with an oxygen absorber for premium retail. For whole pieces sold in bulk, breathable paper bags work for short-term sale but not for long storage. Always label with production date, batch number, and best-before date. Store below 25Â°C and away from direct sunlight.

For drowors, the lower moisture and fermentation acidity give a longer potential shelf life, but fat rancidity is the limiting factor. Keep storage temperatures low and consider nitrogen flushing for export markets. In humid climates, a sachet of silica gel inside bulk cartons helps, but it is not a substitute for correct drying.

6. Business-First Considerations

Biltong is a high-value, low-weight product, which makes it attractive for export and e-commerce. A 1 kg raw beef input at US$5â7 yields 400â500 g of biltong that retails for US$25â40/kg in premium markets. The margin is real, but so are the risks: inconsistent drying, mould losses, and regulatory rejection. Invest first in a reliable drying box and a water activity meter (US$300â600). This single instrument will save you more money than any marketing spend. Second, standardise your spice blend by weight, not by eye. Third, build a simple batch record: raw weight, spice weight, drying time, temperature, RH, final weight, final aw, and sensory notes. After 20 batches you will have a proprietary process that is repeatable, trainable, and financeable.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Raw meat held below 4Â°C and processed within 24 hours of slaughter or thawing.
  • â Salt weighed at 2.5â3.5% of meat weightânever estimated.
  • â Vinegar applied as a surface wash and included in the marinade.
  • â Drying box at 20â27Â°C, RH below 65%, air speed 1â2 m/s.
  • â Final water activity (aw) measured and recorded below 0.85.
  • â Drowors: pH below 5.3 within 48 hours of stuffing.
  • â Batch records kept for every production run (weights, temps, times, aw).
  • â Packaging: vacuum or high-barrier, labelled with batch and best-before date.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Guidelines for the production, processing, labelling and marketing of organically produced foods (relevant to RTE meat handling)
  • WHO/FAO â Guidelines on the Application of General Principles of Food Hygiene to the Control of Listeria monocytogenes in Ready-to-Eat Foods (2007)
  • South African National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications (NRCS) â meat and processed meat regulations
  • USDA National Agricultural Library â Dried Meat Products: Food Safety and Regulatory Resources
  • FAO â Game meat: a review of the industry and its potential (2010)

quiz.q: What is the main role of vinegar in biltong making?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar creates an acidic environment that inhibits bacteria and also helps tenderise the meat.

quiz.q: How much coarse salt is recommended for 1 kg of meat in biltong?
quiz.explanation: The basic recipe uses 20 g coarse salt per 1 kg of meat.

quiz.q: Which spice is traditionally toasted and crushed for biltong?
quiz.explanation: Coriander seeds are toasted and crushed to release their flavour in biltong.

quiz.q: How long should biltong cure in the fridge before drying?
quiz.explanation: The spiced meat is typically refrigerated for 12 to 24 hours to cure.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity range for drying biltong?
quiz.explanation: 50-60% humidity allows slow, even drying without mould growth.

quiz.q: Which cut of beef is best for biltong?
quiz.explanation: Silverside (or topside/rump) is lean and ideal for drying.

quiz.q: What should you do if mould appears on drying biltong?
quiz.explanation: Wipe with vinegar, discard badly affected pieces, and increase airflow to prevent further mould.

quiz.q: How long does beef biltong typically take to dry?
quiz.explanation: Depending on thickness and humidity, biltong dries in 3 to 5 days.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between biltong and droÃ«wors?

quiz.q: Which ingredient is optional in droÃ«wors for tenderness?

quiz.q: How long should droÃ«wors dry in ideal conditions?
quiz.explanation: DroÃ«wors typically dries in 4 to 7 days at 15-20Â°C and 50-60% humidity.

quiz.q: What percentage of fat is recommended when making droÃ«wors from game meat?
quiz.explanation: Adding about 20% beef fat prevents game droÃ«wors from becoming too dry and crumbly.

quiz.q: Why should you prick droÃ«wors with a needle before drying?
quiz.explanation: Pricking releases trapped air, preventing casings from bursting during drying.

quiz.q: Which game animal is known for mild, slightly sweet meat ideal for droÃ«wors?
quiz.explanation: Springbok meat is mild and slightly sweet, making excellent droÃ«wors.

quiz.q: What should you do with game meat before curing?
quiz.explanation: Game fat turns rancid quickly, so it should be trimmed off before curing.

quiz.q: How long should game meat cure compared to beef?
quiz.explanation: Game meat benefits from a slightly longer curing time (up to 36 hours) to tenderise.

quiz.q: Why is game biltong often sold at a premium price?
options: B) It has a stronger flavour
quiz.explanation: Game biltong is prized for its unique flavour, leanness, and limited availability.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for a drying box?
quiz.explanation: 25-30Â°C provides gentle warmth to dry meat without cooking it.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fan in a drying box?
quiz.explanation: The fan circulates air to remove moisture and prevent mould.

quiz.q: How can you lower humidity inside a drying box?
options: A) Add a bowl of water
quiz.explanation: Increasing airflow helps remove moisture and lower humidity.

quiz.explanation: 50-60% humidity is ideal for drying biltong and droÃ«wors without case hardening or mould.

quiz.q: How often should you check meat in a drying box?
quiz.explanation: Checking temperature and humidity twice daily ensures conditions remain optimal.

quiz.q: What is the best material for storing biltong short-term?
quiz.explanation: Paper bags allow breathability and prevent moisture buildup.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid storing biltong in plastic bags?
quiz.explanation: Plastic traps moisture, creating a humid environment where mould grows.

quiz.q: How long can vacuum-sealed biltong last in the freezer?
quiz.explanation: Vacuum-sealed biltong can be frozen for up to 6 months without quality loss.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find mould on stored biltong?
quiz.explanation: Mould can spread invisible spores, so the entire piece should be discarded.

quiz.q: What is a certificate of acceptability (COA)?
quiz.explanation: A COA is a permit from local authorities allowing you to sell processed meat.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for biltong?
quiz.explanation: Cool temperatures below 20Â°C slow spoilage and maintain quality.

quiz.q: Which packaging method is best for long-distance shipping?
quiz.explanation: Vacuum-sealed pouches protect against moisture, air, and contamination during shipping.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label biltong with production and expiry dates?
quiz.explanation: Labels ensure legal compliance, safety, and traceability in case of issues.
